deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated parts: a short integral-calculus fragment at the top, and a numerical Fourier series for the lemniscatic sine below. The continuation (the inverse series in degrees) is on the next page.

(A) Reduction formula. Let I_c = ∫ x^(a-1) dx/(1+x^b)^c. Gauss writes
I_c = x^a/(b(c-1)(1+x^b)^(c-1)) + (bc-a-b)/(bc) · I_(c-1).
Derivation (mine): differentiate x^a(1+x^b)^(1-c) and write x^(a+b-1) = x^(a-1)[(1+x^b)-1]. This gives
d/dx[x^a(1+x^b)^(1-c)] = (a+b-bc) x^(a-1)(1+x^b)^(1-c) + b(c-1) x^(a-1)(1+x^b)^(-c).
Hence I_c = x^a/(b(c-1)(1+x^b)^(c-1)) + (bc-a-b)/(b(c-1)) · I_(c-1).
So the denominator of the second coefficient should be b(c-1), not bc.

He then specialises to a=3, b=4, c=5/4 (so b(c-1)=1 and bc-a-b=-2). He writes ∫ x^2 dx/(1+x^4)^(5/4) = x^3/(1+x^4)^(1/4). This is only the boundary term. The correct statement is
∫ x^2/(1+x^4)^(5/4) dx = x^3/(1+x^4)^(1/4) - 2∫ x^2/(1+x^4)^(1/4) dx.
The lone '∫' on the next line suggests he began writing this remaining term and broke off. The closed form he wrote does hold for a=1: ∫ dx/(1+x^4)^(5/4) = x/(1+x^4)^(1/4). Presumably this connects with lemniscatic-type integrals.

(B) Fourier series of the lemniscatic sine. Here 'sin lemn a' means sl(ϖa/π), so that a = 90° corresponds to the quarter period ϖ/2. ϖ = Γ(1/4)^2/(2√(2π)) = 2.6220575543.

A first rough attempt reads 0.9550060 sin a - 0.0430 sin 3a. The final version is
sl(ϖa/π) = 0.95500599 sin a - 0.04304950 sin 3a + 0.00186048 sin 5a - 0.00008040 sin 7a + 0.00000347 sin 9a - 0.00000015 sin 11a + 0.00000001 sin 13a.
In modern form this is sl(u) = (2π/ϖ) Σ_{n≥0} (-1)^n sin((2n+1)πu/ϖ)/cosh((2n+1)π/2). The coefficients are (2π/ϖ)/cosh((2n+1)π/2), and the successive ratios are about e^(-π) = 0.0432.

Numerical checks on the page:
(i) At a=90° the series gives the sum of the absolute coefficients. This equals 1.00000000 = sl(ϖ/2) (the table entry '1 → 1,').
(ii) At a=45° the signs give c1+c7+c9-c3-c5-c11-c13. His scratch work: 0.95508639 - 0.04490998 = 0.91017641, then +331 gives 0.91017972. He multiplies by √½ = 0.70710678 by partial products (637125804 + 6371258 + 91018 + 6172). The result is 0.64359425 = sl(ϖ/4). Exactly, this is √(√2-1) = 0.6435942529, the table entry '1/2'.
(iii) At a=30°: 2·sl = c1+c5+c7+c11+c13 - 2c3 - 2c9. His work: 0.95694703 - 0.08610594 = 0.87084109, so sl(ϖ/6) = 0.43542054, the table entry '1/3'. A first attempt, 0.52143898 = (0.95500599 + 0.08609900 + 0.00186048 + 0.00000001 - 0.00008752)/2, has the sin 3a term with the wrong sign. It is struck out.

The table is thus sl at fractions 1, 1/2, 1/3 of the quarter period. The next page inverts the series: arcsl as φ + 4.933559° sin 2φ + ....
errors: The reduction formula as written has the coefficient (bc-a-b)/(bc); the correct denominator is b(c-1). This is a slip.

∫x^2 dx/(1+x^4)^(5/4) = x^3/(1+x^4)^(1/4) is false as written: the derivative of the right side is x^2(3+2x^4)/(1+x^4)^(5/4). The correct relation is x^3/(1+x^4)^(1/4) - 2∫x^2 dx/(1+x^4)^(1/4). The line appears unfinished; the stray '∫' follows it.
The first evaluation at 30° (0.52143898) uses the wrong sign for the sin 3a term (+2c3 instead of -2c3). Gauss struck it out and corrected it to 0.43542054.
The first rough series (0.9550060, -0.0430) is a superseded approximation, not an error.

results.what: Reduction formula for ∫x^(a-1)(1+x^b)^(-c)dx lowering c by one
Fourier series sl(ϖa/π) = Σ (-1)^n (2π/ϖ)/cosh((2n+1)π/2) sin((2n+1)a), with 8-digit coefficients
results.modern_name: Fourier expansion of the lemniscatic sine (sn with k^2=-1, via q-series with q=e^(-π))
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (lemniscate researches, c.1797-1800; Werke III/X); Jacobi (1829) for general sn

results.what: Numerical values sl(ϖ/2)=1, sl(ϖ/4)=0.64359425 (=√(√2-1)), sl(ϖ/6)=0.43542054 as checks of the series
results.modern_name: Special values of the lemniscatic sine

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's Fourier expansion of the lemniscatic sine with these numerical coefficients is known from his lemniscate papers (Werke III/X). The integral reduction is textbook Euler. The page is a numerical working sheet with checks.

checkable.asserts: Corrected reduction formula (denominator b(c-1)); should simplify to 0
Nonzero: Gauss's second line is not a complete antiderivative
Duplication of sl(ϖ/6) gives sl(ϖ/3)=(2√3-3)^(1/4); ≈0 confirms 0.43542054
